abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Wave breaking geometry is critical for understanding air‐sea interactions, yet its characterization in the field remains limited. This study analyzes the geometry of 16,369 active breaking waves, measured via stereo imagery in the Black Sea under diverse conditions. We investigate statistical relationships between key geometric properties, including breaking length, height, and speed. Our results reveal that geometric scaling is not constant but varies with the sea state, challenging established empirical models. The data indicate a weak relationship between breaking speed and wave geometry, while internal geometric properties show stronger linear relations. A subsequent test of self‐similarity, based on a heavy‐tailed log‐normal distribution, confirmed its rarity (4%±2% $4\%\pm 2\%$ of events). This comprehensive geometric description underscores that wave breaking properties are sea‐state‐dependent.

abstract.title: Plain Language Summary
abstract.p: Breaking wave geometry has historically been investigated through laboratory studies, with very limited open ocean observations. Understanding wave geometry is key for modeling air‐sea gas exchange, energy dissipation, and satellite measurements. We measured the geometry—including area, length, height, duration, and speed—of over 16,000 breaking waves in the Black Sea. Our analysis reveals that real‐world breaking waves do not conform to a self‐similar geometry, nor are there predictable relationships between a wave's breaking speed and its geometric properties. The results indicate that wave breaking geometry is complex and sea‐state dependent.

listItem.p: Novel field observations of breaking wave geometry from a large stereo‐video data set (N=16,369) $(N=16,369)$ are presented
Geometric parameters scale among themselves but exhibit only weak correlation with breaking speed
Only a small fraction (4%±2%) $(4\%\pm 2\%)$ of events is consistent with self‐similar scaling; geometric properties are sea‐state‐dependent

section.title: Introduction
section.p: Wave breaking is the primary contributor to energy dissipation in the open ocean, being of fundamental importance for geophysical and technological applications. Breaking waves inject bubbles and turbulence into the water column which results in the mixing of surface waters. Wave breaking is, therefore, responsible for driving ocean‐atmosphere gas exchanges and upper‐ocean circulation (Terrill et al., 2001). Despite the foam generated by breaking waves typically covering only a small percentage of the sea surface, it can significantly contribute to increases in microwave brightness temperature signatures over the ocean for moderate to high wind speeds (Guo et al., 2001; Monahan, 2002; Reul & Chapron, 2003; Ross & Cardone, 1974; Smith, 1988; Stogryn, 1972) and significantly modulate measurements of backscatter from radar and satellites (Ericson et al., 1999; Jessup et al., 1990; Lewis & Olin, 1980; Lyzenga & Shuchman, 1983; Trizna & Carlson, 1996). Detailed knowledge of the breaking waves statistics in terms of lateral extension Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$, duration Δtb $\left({\Delta }{t}_{b}\right)$ and speed cb $\left({c}_{b}\right)$, and whitecap (foam) coverage Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$ is, accordingly, required to accurately interpret ocean‐atmosphere processes that control the growth and decay of wind‐waves and the transfer of energy between the ocean and atmosphere (Reul & Chapron, 2003).

A statistical relationship between wave breaking length Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$ and wave phase speed (c) $(c)$ is one of the methods used to investigate breaking waves in the deep water regime. The developments and concepts were originally introduced by Phillips (1985), hereafter P85. This implies that the geometric properties of the breaking waves (e.g., Lb ${L}_{b}$) would scale with the wavelength (λ=2πc2/g $\lambda =2{\uppi }{c}^{2}/g$, in deep waters) of the carrying wave. P85 theory is currently used to investigate different phenomena such as whitecap coverage, rate of air entrainment, momentum flux, and energy dissipation (Gemmrich et al., 2013) but with little validation from field data. Further, in P85's original theory, the speed of the breaking wave is assumed to be equal to that of the carrying wave (i.e., c=cb $c={c}_{b}$) but laboratory (Jessup & Phadnis, 2005; Rapp & Melville, 1990; Stansell & MacFarlane, 2002) and field experiments (Banner, Barthelemy, et al., 2014) showed that cb≈0.8c ${c}_{b}\approx 0.8c$ with low local fluctuations of +7% ${+}7\%$ to −1% ${-}1\%$ (Banner, Barthelemy, et al., 2014).

Based on laboratory experiment Duncan (1981) hereafter D81, described breaking waves to be self‐similar, so their geometrical properties scale accordingly to constants. D81 used a towed hydrofoil to generate and investigate steady breaking waves, and his experiments showed a remarkable correlation between peak phase speed cp $\left({c}_{p}\right)$, the length of the breaking crest Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$, and the amplitude of the breaking wave Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$ (see D81 Figures 5 and 6). He also observed that the ratio between wave breaking area Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$ and wave breaking length squared LD81 $\left({L}_{\mathit{D81}}\right)$ was constant and equal to Ab/LD812=0.11±0.01 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.11\pm 0.01$ for all his data. P85 used D81 constants and his own concepts of spectral equilibrium and saturation to directly correlate energy dissipation due to wave breaking to the geometry of the breaking waves. More recently, a study by Caulliez (2002) seemed to demonstrated evidence for wave self‐similarity but this author only investigated a very limited range of wave ages (cp/u∗ ${c}_{p}/{u}_{\ast }$, where u∗ ${u}_{\ast }$ is the wind shear velocity) and did not explicitly identified breaking waves (he instead used a empirical maximum slope criteria). A linear scale wave‐breaking is often used to investigate the dynamics of whitecap coverage (Callaghan, 2018; Callaghan et al., 2016; Rapp & Melville, 1990; Reul & Chapron, 2003) with direct application on empirical models for satellites radar backscatter and microwave brightness temperature signatures (Kudryavtsev et al., 2003; Monahan, 2002; Reul & Chapron, 2003). However, to the authors' understanding, there are still very limited field experiment that investigates wave breaking geometries at natural seas.

Therefore, this paper's primary objective is to investigate the geometrical properties of wind‐generated breaking waves using a relatively large field data set. To this end, we investigate in detail the properties of the active wave breaking area Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$, breaking wave crest length Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$, lateral eA $\left({e}_{A}\right)$ and cross wave eB $\left({e}_{B}\right)$ foam extensions, wave breaking duration Δtb $\left({\Delta }{t}_{b}\right)$ and wave breaking speed cb $\left({c}_{b}\right)$. The results obtained here will have important implications in several areas of research such as wave modeling and forecasting, ocean‐atmosphere interactions, and remote sensing of the ocean. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the data set and the active wave breaking detection method, Section 3 presents the results, Section 4 discusses and Section 5 concludes. We also make all our data available alongside this publication.

section.title: Field Data
section.p: The wave breaking data set was constructed from 20 stereo video acquisitions recorded at the Marine Hydrophysical Institute platform in the Black Sea, 500 m off the Katsiveli coast (44.39° $39{}^{\circ}$N, 33.98° $98{}^{\circ}$E). The water depth at the observation area is approximately 30 m. The stereo video system was mounted 11 m above the sea surface and used a pair of synchronized 5 Megapixel (2,048 × 2,456 pixels) BM‐500 GE JAI cameras equipped with wide‐angle lenses. The cameras were installed on the eastern corner of the deck of the platform, pointing to a direction 82° $82{}^{\circ}$ clockwise of North. The sea state conditions during the acquisitions were dominated by wind seas with a wide range of wind speeds and directions which resulted in fetches ranging from 1,000 km (i.e., across the Black Sea) to 500 m (northerly wind conditions). A description of the experimental conditions are detailed in Table 1. The stereo video reconstruction was done as per Benetazzo (2006), Benetazzo et al. (2012) and Leckler (2013). A detailed validation of the stereo video is presented by Guimarães (2018) and, when compared to a wave gauge, the stereo video reconstruction presented a good spectral agreement up to 1.4 Hz. For further details regarding data collection, see Guimarães (2018); Guimaraes et al. (2020).

section.title: Wave Breaking Detection
section.p: The wave breaking detection method used for this study was based on the automatic foam identification method from Mironov and Dulov (2008). This method aims to eliminate human influence in foam detection by defining a fixed pixel intensity (I) $(I)$ threshold for whitecap identification. Further, the method makes a distinction between waves that are actively breaking and passive foam. An active wave breaking event is defined as the part of the foam patch that is expanding in time and is moving at speeds greater than one m per second. All other instances of bright pixels that do not meet these requirements are considered passive foam. For further detail regarding this method applied to the same data see Leckler (2013) and Guimarães (2018). The automatic detection method initially identified 22,116 active wave breaking events over the 20 stereo video records. It was observed, however, that a significant amount of passive foam and other instances of bright pixels (e.g., sun glints) were being identified as active wave breaking. To avoid the propagation of errors into the analyses, all detected wave breaking events were manually inspected, and incorrect data were removed from the data set, resulting in a total of 16,369 active wave breaking events. Events were retained only when the foam patch exhibited continuous spatial expansion over at least three consecutive frames and when the barycenter velocity exceeded 1 m s−1 ${\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$, consistent with the active‐breaking criterion of Mironov and Dulov (2008). False positives (stationary sun glints, birds, fragmented noise patches) were discarded. This procedure is consistent with the manual quality‐control applied in comparable optical studies (Banner, Zappa, & Gemmrich, 2014; Kleiss & Melville, 2011). Combined with the stereo video measurements, it is possible to compute the space and time evolution of the actively breaking foam in metric coordinates. Individual breaking events were defined as foam pixels connected in both space and time: pixels in consecutive frames were associated with the same event via connected‐component labeling (Kleiss & Melville, 2011), and a new event was initiated when a foam patch appeared more than 1 m from any existing active patch. This “per‐event” approach differs from “per‐frame” counting and focuses on the geometric properties of individual breaking episodes; the implications of this choice are discussed by Banner, Zappa, and Gemmrich (2014). Each wave breaking event corresponds, therefore, to “white” pixels connected in space and time (i.e., I(t,x,y,z) $I(t,x,y,z)$). Note that this method does not include micro‐scale wave breaking as they do not produce enough foam to be detected by Mironov and Dulov's (2008) thresholding method.

section.title: Wave Breaking Geometry Definitions
section.p:
The main geometric properties of each active wave breaking event were computed as follows. At each time step, the contour of each wave breaking event was extracted using the α $\alpha $‐shape method (Edelsbrunner et al., 1983) using the implementation from Bellock (2019). This method constructs a non‐convex enclosure on the set of points I(x,y) $I(x,y)$ and depends on the free‐parameter α $\alpha $. For the data investigated here, a value of α $\alpha $ = 20 was found by visual inspection. From the α $\alpha $‐shape geometry, the wave breaking area Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$, length Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$ and barycenter (bc(x,y)) $(bc(x,y))$ were recorded. Further, a minimum enclosing ellipse (Moshtagh, 2005) was fitted to each event and the cross‐wave eA $\left({e}_{A}\right)$ and along‐wave eB $\left({e}_{B}\right)$ lengths (corresponding to the major and minor axes of the ellipse, respectively) were recorded. The vertical foam extension Δzb $\left({\Delta }{z}_{b}\right)$ was obtained directly from the three‐dimensional structure of the foam patch (i.e., from I(x,y,z) $I(x,y,z)$). Finally, the wave breaking speed cb $\left({c}_{b}\right)$ was calculated as displacement over time considering the barycenter positions in adjacent timesteps. The use of barycenter speed as a proxy for breaking speed follows previous studies (e.g., Kleiss & Melville, 2011; Sutherland & Melville, 2013), though we recognize that it may not perfectly represent the propagation speed of the breaking crest front, especially for irregular and evolving foam patches. We tested alternative definitions, such as the initial speed at the onset of breaking and the speed projected onto the major axis of the ellipse, but found that they did not reduce the scatter in the relationships (see Section 3). This suggests that the weak correlation between cb ${c}_{b}$ and geometric parameters is robust to the choice of speed definition. Note that these parameters can be obtained as averages, maxima in time, or summed during the wave breaking event duration. A list of variables is defined below and Figure 1 exemplifies the geometric properties being investigated here.
cb ${c}_{b}$—Mean wave breaking speed ms−1 $\left({\mathrm{ms}}^{-1}\right)$
c0 ${c}_{0}$—Initial wave breaking speed ms−1 $\left({\mathrm{ms}}^{-1}\right)$
ce ${c}_{e}$—Mean wave breaking speed in the direction orthogonal to eA ${e}_{A}$ ms−1 $\left({\mathrm{ms}}^{-1}\right)$
Ab ${A}_{b}$—Maximum wave breaking covered area (equivalent to foam coverage) m2 $\left({\mathrm{m}}^{2}\right)$
Lb ${L}_{b}$—Maximum wave breaking length amplitude (0.5 × perimeter from α $\alpha $‐shape) (m) $(\mathrm{m})$
LD81 ${L}_{\mathit{D81}}$—Wave breaking length as per Duncan (1981) (m) $(\mathrm{m})$
eA ${e}_{A}$—Maximum across‐wave length (i.e., major ellipse axis) (m) $(\mathrm{m})$
eB ${e}_{B}$—Maximum along‐wave length (i.e., minor ellipse axis) (m) $(\mathrm{m})$
Δzb ${\Delta }{z}_{b}$—Vertical foam extension (m) $(\mathrm{m})$
θ $\theta $—Angle of inclination of the wave's forward face (Duncan, 1981) (o)
Δtb ${\Delta }{t}_{b}$—Event duration (s) $(\mathrm{s})$

section.title: Results
section.p: Our analyses start with the description of the probability density function (PDF) of six parameters used to describe breaking waves (Figure 2). Although these parameters are frequently used to describe breaking waves, their natural variability has not yet been described. All analyzed parameters (presented at Section 2.3) were statistically similar to a log‐normal PDF (Dodge, 2008) when tested using the two‐tail Kolmogorov‐Smirnov at the 95% confidence level (Massey Jr, 1951). Further, the log‐normal distribution was the best ranking PDF to model the data when compared to all other distributions available in the scipy library (Virtanen et al., 2020) if assessed using the Akaike Information Criteria (Akaike, 1974). The PDF of the wave breaking area at its maximum extent during each wave breaking event Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$ normalized by the square of the peak wavelength (λp ${\lambda }_{p}$ = g2πTp2 $\frac{g}{2{\uppi }}{T}_{p}^{2}$) and the PDF of the wave breaking length at maximum extent Lb ${L}_{b}$ normalized by λp ${\lambda }_{p}$ are shown in Figures 2a and 2b. These two variables present remarkably heavy tails, which be investigated in further detail below. The PDF of the angle of inclination of the wave's forward face (θ $\theta $) calculated as per D81 is shown in Figure 2c. The range of θ $\theta $ observed here (3° $3{}^{\circ}$ to 71° $71{}^{\circ}$) is significantly wider than the range reported by D81 (10° $10{}^{\circ}$ to 14.7° $7{}^{\circ}$) but the peak of the distribution matches D81's observations. The aspect ratio parameter Ab/LD812 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}$ shown in Figure 2d also has a wide range of variability, peaked at 0.46 and had an average of 0.56±0.26 $0.56\pm 0.26$. For comparison, Duncan (1981) reported Ab/LD812=0.11±0.01 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.11\pm 0.01$ (coefficient of variation ≈9%) under controlled laboratory conditions, consistent with self‐similar geometry. The coefficient of variation of approximately 46% found here indicates a substantially wider distribution and a departure from strict geometric self‐similarity. The wave breaking duration Δtb $\left({\Delta }{t}_{b}\right)$ normalized by wave peak period Tp $\left({T}_{p}\right)$ (Figure 2e) exhibited a stepped distribution with substantial scatter, primarily attributable to the finite frame rate (10–15 Hz) of the stereo acquisitions, which limits the temporal resolution of event duration to increments of 0.07–0.10 s; a similar artifact has been reported in other optical breaking‐wave studies (Kleiss & Melville, 2011). This PDF indicates that the active part of the wave breaking is only a small fraction of the total wave period. Finally, the PDF of the ratio between wave breaking speed and wave phase speed (cb/cp ${c}_{b}/{c}_{p}$, Figure 2‐f) showed that wave breaking crests travel at speeds much slower than the peak wave speed, which is consistent with previous results (Gemmrich et al., 2008) and with the field observations of Banner, Barthelemy, et al. (2014), who reported cb≈0.8c ${c}_{b}\approx 0.8c$.

section.p: Figures 3a–3c present analyses analogous to those of D81. Figure 3‐a shows the scatter plot between the along‐wave crest length Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$ and cb ${c}_{b}$; Figure 3b is equivalent to Figure 5 in Duncan (1981) and shows the scatter plot between the cross‐wave length LD81 $\left({L}_{\mathit{D81}}\right)$ and cb ${c}_{b}$; Figure 3c is equivalent to Figure 7 in D81 and shows the scatter plot between the vertical foam extent (Δzb ${\Delta }{z}_{b}$, assumed equivalent to LD81sinθ ${L}_{\mathit{D81}}\,\sin \,\theta $) and cb ${c}_{b}$. Compared to D81's results, the data analyzed here had a much higher degree of scatter, but qualitatively similar quadratic relationships (green lines) could be retrieved. The fitted relations, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, are: Lb=(0.83±0.04)cb2/g ${L}_{b}=(0.83\pm 0.04){c}_{b}^{2}/g$, LD81=(0.66±0.04)cb2/g ${L}_{\mathit{D81}}=(0.66\pm 0.04){c}_{b}^{2}/g$, and Δzb=(0.20±0.02)cb2/g ${\Delta }{z}_{b}=(0.20\pm 0.02){c}_{b}^{2}/g$ (where g=9.81 $g=9.81$ m s−2 ${\mathrm{s}}^{-2}$). Different strategies to estimate the characteristic wave breaking speed, for instance, by taking it as the speed at the onset of breaking (c0 ${c}_{0}$, as recommended by Gemmrich et al. (2013)) or by considering only the speed component in the eB ${e}_{B}$ direction ce $\left({c}_{e}\right)$, did not reduce the degree of scatter (Pearson r<0.45 $r< 0.45$ in all cases), consistent with the findings of Kleiss and Melville (2011) and Sutherland and Melville (2013). Similar weak relations were found when Lb ${L}_{b}$ was replaced by eB ${e}_{B}$, eA ${e}_{A}$, Ab ${A}_{b}$, or Δzb ${\Delta }{z}_{b}$ (not shown).

section.p: The correlation score was much more significant for variables related to the breaking geometry themselves. We found a significant correlation between foam area, breaking length and vertical extension, rAb,Lb=0.9 $r\left({A}_{b},{L}_{b}\right)=0.9$, rAb,LD81=0.8 $r\left({A}_{b},\,{L}_{\mathit{D81}}\right)=0.8$, rΔzbmax,eBmax=0.7 $r\left({\Delta }{z}_{{b}_{\max }},\,{e}_{{B}_{\max }}\right)=0.7$. A relation between between foam coverage Ab ${A}_{b}$ and breaking extension LD812 ${L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}$ (Figure 3d was inspired in D81 (where Ab/LD812=0.11 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.11$). From our data set Ab/LD812=0.22 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.22$, and Ab/Lb2=0.27 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{b}^{2}=0.27$, with r $r$ around 0.8 to 0.9 and p−value≪0.05 $p-value\ll 0.05$ for all these cases. Those relations are particularly useful in the estimation of the whitecap coverage, rate of air entrainment, moment flux, and energy dissipated.

Figure 3e presents a relation between the lateral and cross extension of the breaking foam using the ellipses fitting major and minor axis (eA/eB=2.37 ${e}_{A}/{e}_{B}=2.37$ for r=0.8 $r=0.8$). A relation between the foam coverage and the ellipse fitting area Ae $\left({A}_{e}\right)$ is given by Ae=2.5Ab ${A}_{e}=2.5{A}_{b}$ with a correlation index of r=0.9 $r=0.9$, this relation is particular useful depending on the characteristics of the data acquired and processed. The linear relation between breaking duration and foam coverage, foam extension also presented small correlation, rAb,Δtb=0.6 $r\left({A}_{b},{\Delta }{t}_{b}\right)=0.6$, rLb,Δtb=0.5 $r\left({L}_{b},{\Delta }{t}_{b}\right)=0.5$ and rΔzb,Δtb=0.4 $r\left({\Delta }{z}_{b},{\Delta }{t}_{b}\right)=0.4$ (Figure 3f).

The trends and correlations analyzed were also sensitive to the methodology applied to compute these variables, as previously observed by (Banner, Zappa, & Gemmrich, 2014; Kleiss & Melville, 2011). Despite some linear or non‐linear trends between wave breaking speed and breaking geometry could be found in laboratory experiments and at sea, the statistical correlation between wave breaking geometry and wave breaking speed was considerably small in our data set at natural sea. A simple deterministic relation between these wave breaking properties may carry a significant error in the same order of magnitude or higher than the estimated variable. In these cases, a probabilistic approach might be a better representation of the observed data. A statistical analysis based on Patel and Schoenberg (2011) heavy‐tailed self‐similarity test is discussed below.

section.title: Discussion
section.p: As stated in the introduction, it is widely assumed that breaking waves are self‐similar, meaning that smaller breakers are merely scaled copies of larger ones. Following Barenblatt (1996), geometric self‐similarity requires that the non‐dimensional shape parameters of breaking events (such as Ab/LD812 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}$, Δzb/Lb ${\Delta }{z}_{b}/{L}_{b}$, and Lb/λ ${L}_{b}/\lambda $) remain invariant under rescaling by a characteristic length. Duncan (1981) demonstrated this property in laboratory experiments where Ab/LD812=0.11±0.01 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.11\pm 0.01$ (coefficient of variation ≈9%) across all tested conditions. In contrast, our field data yield Ab/LD812=0.56±0.26 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.56\pm 0.26$ (coefficient of variation ≈46%), indicating that strict geometric self‐similarity is not a general property of wind‐sea breaking waves. In addition, we apply a complementary statistical test: A stochastic process is self‐similar with Hurst index H $H$ if its finite‐dimensional distributions are invariant under an appropriate rescaling of space and time (Embrechts & Maejima, 2002). For such processes with heavy‐tailed marginal distributions, the complementary cumulative distribution function (1–CDF) decays as a power law, which manifests as a straight line on a log‐log plot (Clauset et al., 2009).

Following the graphical approach of Patel and Schoenberg (2011), it is possible to check for self‐similarity by plotting the 1–CDF against the random variable on log‐log axes; a linear trend indicates scale invariance. This approach is equivalent to the power‐law tail detection method of Clauset et al. (2009), who applied it to a broad range of geophysical and physical data sets. We cross‐checked our results using the maximum‐likelihood fitting procedure of Clauset et al. (2009) and obtained consistent conclusions. Typical examples of heavy‐tailed distributions consistent with self‐similar behavior include the Pareto (Arnold, 2015) and log‐normal (Dodge, 2008) PDFs. Figure 4 shows the application of this technique to variables describing the wave breaking area (Ab ${A}_{b}$, Figure 4a), crest length (Lb ${L}_{b}$, Figure 4b) and aspect ratio (Ab/LD812 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}$, Figure 4c). The Pareto fit (green line) does not appear as a straight line on the log‐log plot because the data do not follow a pure power law over the full range of the distribution; the deviation from linearity indicates that heavy‐tailed behavior is limited to the extreme tail, consistent with a log‐normal rather than a Pareto parent distribution (Dodge, 2008). From the analyses of Figures 4a–4c, none of the analyzed variables could be considered fully self‐similar over their entire range. It is noteworthy, however, that the tails of these distributions—especially the tail of Ab/LD812 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}$—do approximate a straight line (solid black lines in Figure 4), which, taken in isolation, could be considered indicative of self‐similar behavior.

section.p: From the Patel and Schoenberg (2011) test, only 4% of the breaking events could be considered self‐similar. The green dots and lines at Figure 4d to f represent the data contained in the linear fit of tail of the distribution or the breaking events that could be considered self‐similar. The data presented a variance of ± $\pm $2% of self‐similar wave breaking events depending on the sea state condition and variable analyzed. The physical interpretation of this test is that only smaller and faster wave breaking events resemble each other and, therefore, were considered self‐similar (Figure 4d). Those wave breaking events also tend to a produce larger amount of foam and consequently cover a larger surface area Ab $\left({A}_{b}\right)$ when compared to most of other breaking events at the same breaking length Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$ (Figures 4e and 4f).

In contrast, the remaining 96% of breaking events could not be considered self‐similar based on the Patel and Schoenberg (2011) inverse CDF test. These results do not preclude the possibility that self‐similarity may hold within narrower subsets of the data, for instance, under a restricted range of wave ages or wind speeds, but a dedicated stratified analysis would be required to test this hypothesis and is beyond the scope of the present study. The observed record‐to‐record variability in the fitted coefficients (Table 1), together with the scatter in the pooled relations, is consistent with the sea‐state dependence of breaking statistics reported by Kleiss and Melville (2011) and Banner, Zappa, and Gemmrich (2014). We therefore caution against applying constant scaling laws derived from controlled laboratory experiments to the full range of oceanic conditions without further validation.

Several physical mechanisms may contribute to the departure from self‐similarity observed here. Short‐wave steepness in a natural sea is a multi‐scale problem: the orbital velocities and apparent gravity of longer waves modulate the steepness and action of shorter waves, progressively concentrating short‐wave energy near the crests of longer waves (Guimarães, 2018; Peureux et al., 2020). The space–time evolution of wave crest steepness at short wavelengths is a nonlinear function of the phase, speed, amplitude, and direction of the interacting wave components (Zhang & Melville, 1992). For cb<cp ${c}_{b}< {c}_{p}$, a breaking crest propagates more slowly than the underlying longer wave group and may be inhomogeneously modulated by it; moreover, longer wave crests do not necessarily propagate in the same direction as the breaking crest, so a steepness gradient can develop along the breaking front, producing variability in the shape and propagation speed of the breaking region. A quantitative theoretical treatment of this mechanism (without breaking) is provided by Peureux et al. (2020). Additionally, local wind speed and direction can produce a nonlinear response in the wave field and influence wave breaking (Hara et al., 2003; Hasselmann et al., 1985; Keller & Wright, 1975). These factors collectively explain the wide scatter in geometric ratios and the rarity of self‐similar events in a natural, multi‐scale sea.

section.title: Conclusions
section.p: This paper has presented a comprehensive statistical analysis of the geometric properties of wave breaking events observed under natural sea conditions (N=16,369 $N=16,369$ observations). Several geometric variables (e.g., Lb ${L}_{b}$, LD81 ${L}_{\mathit{D81}}$, Δzb ${\Delta }{z}_{b}$, Ab ${A}_{b}$, eB ${e}_{B}$, eA ${e}_{A}$) were found to be well described by a log‐normal PDF, as confirmed by the two‐tailed Kolmogorov‐Smirnov test at the 95% confidence level (Massey Jr, 1951). The aspect ratio Ab/LD812=0.56±0.26 ${A}_{b}/{L}_{\mathit{D81}}^{2}=0.56\pm 0.26$ observed in the field data set is substantially more variable than the laboratory value of 0.11±0.01 $0.11\pm 0.01$ reported by Duncan (1981), quantitatively demonstrating the departure from strict geometric self‐similarity. Only a marginal correlation between wave breaking speed cb $\left({c}_{b}\right)$ and breaking crest length Lb $\left({L}_{b}\right)$ was found (gLb/cb2=0.83±0.04 $g{L}_{b}/{c}_{b}^{2}=0.83\pm 0.04$ for r=0.4 $r=0.4$), consistent with the scatter‐dominated field observations of Kleiss and Melville (2011) and Sutherland and Melville (2013). The hypothesis of breaking self‐similarity was tested using the graphical approach of Patel and Schoenberg (2011), cross‐validated with the maximum‐likelihood method of Clauset et al. (2009). The results indicated that only 4%±2% $4\%\pm 2\%$ of the detected wave breaking events are consistent with self‐similar scaling. For this subset of the data, the correlation between cb ${c}_{b}$ and Lb ${L}_{b}$ improves significantly (gLb/cb2=0.30 $g{L}_{b}/{c}_{b}^{2}=0.30$ for r=0.9 $r=0.9$). We acknowledge that a demonstration of explicit sea‐state dependence would require a dedicated stratified analysis by Hs ${H}_{s}$, Tp ${T}_{p}$, or wave age, which is beyond the scope of this study. In general, the results indicate that constant geometric scaling assumptions commonly used in operational wave models, derived from controlled laboratory experiments or limited sea‐state conditions, should be treated with caution and re‐evaluated against broader field data sets.
